newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration defends chemical arms treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration defends chemical arms treaty.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Sunday defended the Chemical Weapons Convention from attack by a key Senator who has vowed to block U.S. ratification of the treaty unless it is substantially modified.

"This treaty is very much in our interest," Defence Secretary William Cohen said on NBC Television's "Meet the Press" programme. "Whether it's ratified or not, we're out of the business of making chemical weapons."

"We will be worse off as far as the American people are concerned about trying to gain control over the proliferation of chemical weapons throughout the world," if the Senate does not ratify the treaty, Cohen said.
White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles made the same point on ABC Television's "This Week" programme.
"We strongly believe the United States should ratify this convention," he said.
They were responding to Sen. Jesse Helms' vow to bottle up the treaty in his committee unless President Bill Clinton's administration agrees to major modifications which he did not spell out.

The North Carolina Republican, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, told an annual conference of the Conservative Political Action Conference on Saturday that he would prevent the treaty from going to the full Senate for a vote.
The convention outlawing chemical weapons has been ratified more than 60 nations and is due to take effect on April 29 with or without the United States.
Helms maintains that the treaty cannot be verified and that nations who do not sign it such as North Korea, Syria, Libya and Iraq can continue to do as they please.

Helms also complained that the treaty would mean that U.S. companies would have to turn over secrets of their technology and "lull the world into a false sense of security ... when in fact nothing is being done."
